source.name: ASTRA Bio wave 1 — Enzymes
source.license: Original syllabus-based practice questions (exam-frequent themes; not verbatim past papers)

questions.stem: Almost all enzymes in living cells are chemically
questions.explanation: Most enzymes are proteins; a few catalytic RNAs (ribozymes) are the exception.

questions.stem: An enzyme speeds a metabolic reaction mainly by
options: adding heat until the mixture boils
questions.explanation: The catalyst lowers the energy barrier so more molecules react at cell temperature.

questions.stem: The pocket on an enzyme that binds the substrate is called the
questions.explanation: Substrate binds at the active site to form a transient enzyme–substrate complex.

questions.stem: Above a high temperature, enzyme activity falls sharply because the protein is
questions.explanation: Heat unfolds the tertiary structure, so the active site is lost.

questions.stem: Km of an enzyme is the substrate concentration at which velocity is
questions.explanation: Michaelis constant Km equals [S] at 1/2 Vmax and is an inverse measure of affinity.

questions.stem: A competitive inhibitor usually resembles the enzyme's
questions.explanation: It occupies the active site because it is structurally similar to the substrate.

questions.stem: Enzymes that catalyse hydrolysis of bonds are placed in the class
questions.explanation: Hydrolases add water to cleave bonds (e.g. peptidases, amylase).

questions.stem: A loosely bound organic helper that leaves after catalysis is a
questions.explanation: Coenzymes such as NAD, NADP and CoA bind transiently; prosthetic groups stay tightly attached.

questions.stem: The suffix commonly used in systematic enzyme names is
questions.explanation: Enzyme names typically end in -ase (hexokinase, dehydrogenase).

questions.stem: Feedback inhibition typically means the end product of a pathway
options: inhibits an earlier enzyme of the same path
raises Km of every enzyme in the cell
questions.explanation: The end product binds an early (often allosteric) enzyme and slows its own synthesis.

questions.stem: Competitive inhibition of an enzyme can be overcome by
questions.explanation: Extra substrate outcompetes the inhibitor at the active site; Vmax can still be reached.

questions.stem: Each enzyme has a characteristic pH optimum because
options: ionisation of active-site residues changes with pH
enzymes work only at pH 7 in every tissue
pH replaces the need for a substrate
questions.explanation: Charge on catalytic residues and the substrate depends on pH, so binding and catalysis peak at one value.

questions.stem: A low Km value for a given substrate indicates that the enzyme has
questions.explanation: Half-maximal speed is reached at a low [S], so the enzyme binds that substrate tightly.

questions.stem: Ribozymes differ from most cellular enzymes because they are
questions.explanation: 23S rRNA and RNase P are RNA catalysts; nearly all other enzymes are proteins.

questions.stem: On an energy-profile diagram the enzyme-catalysed path shows a
options: changed overall free-energy difference of the reaction
questions.explanation: Enzymes lower Ea but do not alter ΔG or the equilibrium position of the reaction.

questions.stem: According to the induced-fit idea, substrate binding
questions.explanation: Koshland’s induced fit: the active site moulds around the substrate for better catalysis.

questions.stem: A typical human enzyme shows peak activity near
questions.explanation: Animal enzymes are usually optimised near 37 °C; higher heat denatures them.

questions.stem: If substrate is increased while enzyme amount is fixed, velocity
options: stays exactly constant from the start
questions.explanation: Once every active site is occupied, extra substrate cannot raise the rate further.

questions.stem: A non-competitive inhibitor typically binds
options: at a site other than the active site
questions.explanation: It changes enzyme shape from a second site, so Vmax falls and extra substrate cannot fully rescue activity.

questions.stem: Transferases are enzymes that
options: move a group from one molecule to another
questions.explanation: Transferases shift a functional group (e.g. kinases transfer phosphate).

questions.stem: The complete catalytically active enzyme plus its cofactor is the
questions.explanation: Apoenzyme is the protein alone; holoenzyme is protein + cofactor.

questions.stem: Lock-and-key specificity means an enzyme
options: acts equally on many unrelated substrates
acts on one substrate or a few closely related ones
questions.explanation: Fischer’s lock-and-key picture explains why each enzyme recognises a particular substrate shape.

questions.stem: An allosteric modulator binds
options: reversibly at a site distinct from the active site
only to the substrate in free solution
questions.explanation: Allosteric effectors change activity by binding a regulatory site, not the catalytic pocket.

questions.stem: Which statement about competitive inhibition is correct?
options: Vmax decreases and Km is unchanged
Vmax is unchanged but apparent Km increases
both Vmax and Km fall to zero
the inhibitor binds only after the product leaves
questions.explanation: More substrate is needed to reach the same Vmax, so apparent Km rises; Vmax itself is unchanged.

questions.stem: Haem that remains tightly attached to catalase is best called a
questions.explanation: A prosthetic group is an organic cofactor bound permanently (or very tightly) to the protein.

questions.stem: Which pairing of enzyme class and reaction type is incorrect?
options: Ligases — bond formation coupled to ATP
questions.explanation: Redox reactions are catalysed by oxidoreductases; hydrolases cleave bonds by adding water.
